As a noun, "ill" means harm, evil, trouble, or misfortune — anything that is bad, damaging, or painful, whether for a person, a community, or the world. Think of it simply as "something bad."

"Ill" as a noun exists in two forms, and each is used a little differently.

1. Singular "ill" (uncountable — general harm or evil)

In this form, "ill" refers to harm or evil in an abstract, general sense. You're not pointing to a specific list of bad things — just the broad idea of harm, damage, or wrongdoing.

It almost always appears with the word "no" or in a small set of fixed phrases.

Examples:

  • "I wish you no ill." → I don't wish any harm upon you.
  • "He meant no ill." → He had no harmful intention.
  • "She bore him no ill." → She held no hostility or resentment toward him.
  • "For good or ill, the decision is final." → Whether the outcome turns out to be good or bad, the decision stands. (This is a fixed expression — explained further below.)

In these sentences, "ill" works exactly like words such as "harm" or "evil" — it's a thing, but an abstract and uncountable one. You wouldn't say "an ill" or "two ills" in this usage.

2. Plural "ills" (countable — specific problems or harmful things)

This is the more common form in modern English. When we say "the ills of something," we mean the specific, individual problems or harmful realities connected to it. These are concrete and countable — you can imagine listing them one by one.

Examples:

  • "Poverty is one of the great ills of our society." → Poverty is one of the serious, deep-rooted problems of our society.
  • "She devoted her life to fighting the ills of injustice and inequality." → She fought the specific harmful realities of injustice and inequality.
  • "Politicians must address the ills of a broken healthcare system." → They must deal with the specific problems that are harming the system.
  • "The doctor tried to cure the patient's many ills." → The doctor tried to address all of the patient's ailments and sufferings.

Notice that "ills" can refer to social problems, moral wrongs, or physical suffering — whatever category of "bad things" the context is pointing to.

Whether singular or plural, "ill" as a noun always carries the same weight: something that is harmful, wrong, or causing suffering. The distinction is simple:

  • Singular "ill" = harm in general (abstract, usually in fixed phrases)
  • Plural "ills" = specific, individual harms or problems (used more freely)

"Ill" as a noun is formal and literary. You will not hear it in casual, everyday conversation. It belongs to formal writing, journalism, political speeches, serious literature, and moral or philosophical discussion.

When someone says "the ills of modern capitalism" rather than "the problems of modern capitalism," they are consciously choosing a grander, weightier word — one that implies not just inconvenience, but genuine moral or human damage. This is the word's power: it sounds serious and serious things deserve it.

"For good or ill"
This is a well-known fixed phrase meaning "regardless of whether the result is good or bad." It acknowledges that an outcome is uncertain — or that it has already happened and cannot be changed — but that it will be accepted either way.

  • "For good or ill, social media has transformed how people connect." → Whether that transformation is ultimately positive or negative, it has happened.
  • "For good or ill, she had made her choice." → Her choice was made, whatever consequences it might bring.

"Wish someone no ill"
A formal way of saying you hold no hostility, resentment, or harmful intent toward someone.

  • "Despite our disagreement, I wish him no ill."

"Mean no ill"
Used to clarify that an action or statement was not intended to cause harm.

  • "I meant no ill by the remark — I simply didn't know."

"Harm" — The closest everyday equivalent. "I wish you no harm" and "I wish you no ill" mean the same thing, but "ill" sounds more formal and literary.

"Evil" — Stronger and more moral in tone. "Evil" suggests deep moral corruption or wickedness. "Ill" is simply bad or harmful — it carries no implication of extreme moral wrongness.

"Trouble" — Casual and everyday. "Troubles" and "ills" can overlap, but "ills" sounds grander, more serious, and carries a deeper moral weight.

"Problems" — The most ordinary word. "Social problems" and "social ills" often mean the same thing, but "social ills" has a heavier, more formal register — it implies that real human suffering is involved, not just inconveniences.
One important thing to watch for

In older texts — literature from centuries past — you may see "ills" used to mean physical ailments or sicknesses (what we would today simply call "illnesses"). For example: "He suffered many ills in his old age" could, in an older context, mean he suffered many physical sicknesses.

In modern English, this usage is rare and sounds archaic. Today, when someone uses "ills" as a noun, they almost always mean social, moral, or situational problems — not medical conditions. If someone means physical illness, they will say "illness," "sickness," or "ailment."
